activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: An obituary is a published notice of someone's death that usually includes a short account of their life, such as their family, work and interests.
story:
The paper was folded into eighths in Gabriella's jacket pocket, and every few minutes she took it out again and smoothed it on her knee. In the front seat, her mother drove with both hands on the wheel and the radio off, which was how you could tell this was a serious day. "Read it to me one more time," her mother said at the second red light, so Gabriella unfolded the page and read the box at the bottom, the one with Grandpa's name at the top in bold.

"William Torres, age seventy-nine. He is survived by his daughter Rosa and his granddaughter Gabriella." She paused, because the next part still surprised her. "Before his long career as a high school janitor, he served four years as a sailor." She looked up. "Mom. A sailor. He never said one word about that. Not ever."

"Sixty years, Gabi. People put things away that long ago." Her mother's voice was careful, the way it had been all week, as if she was afraid of dropping something.

Gabriella had a theory, and she tested it the way she tested things, quietly and with evidence. She pulled up the newspaper website on her phone and scrolled through the other notices on the same page, the contemporary ones, printed that very morning. There was a woman who had worked thirty years as a nurse, loved by her three sons and her church choir. There was a man who collected stamps and was survived by his wife of fifty years. Every single box told who the person was to their family, what work they had done, and what they had cared about. That was the whole point of it, she realized. An obituary was a published notice of someone's death, but it was also a short account of a whole life, told in public, whether or not the person had ever told it to you themselves.

She texted Cynthia, because Cynthia's grandmother had died last spring and Cynthia would know. "Did you know your grandma taught piano before the restaurant thing?" The answer came back fast: "NO?? nobody tells us anything." Then Malorie wrote, "It's like there's a secret file on every grandparent and you only get to open it at the end." Gabriella looked at that for a long moment. It felt almost true, and it also felt like the opposite of what she wanted.

"I should have asked him things," she said out loud. "All those Sunday dinners, I just talked about school."

Her mother reached over and squeezed her hand, a small act of compassion that made the next words easier. "He liked your school stories. But Gabi, he had sixty more years than you. You couldn't have anticipated what was in them." Gabriella thought about arguing that she could have tried, then decided the question would stay open, the way a drawer stays half shut.

At the cemetery gates, a man in a navy cap was waiting by the doors, and when her mother hugged him, he said, "Billy's old crew sends this." He held out a folded flag with an anchor stitched in the corner. Gabriella took it in both hands. "Tell me about the ship," she said.

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: In Python, the % operator gives the remainder of a division, so n % d == 0 is true exactly when d divides n evenly.
story:
Maria had promised Ms. Krause a working prime-checker by Saturday, which meant she had five days to figure out how a computer could possibly know that 17 was prime and 18 was not. Computers could not look at a number and just see it, the way people did. They had to be told every step, and Maria did not yet know the steps herself. She had claimed the corner computer at the public library, next to the window, with her notebook open to a page that said, in increasingly desperate handwriting, how does it KNOW?

Jet slid into the chair beside her and read the page upside down. "You could just make a list of all the primes and check if the number's on it."

"All of them?"

"Is that a lot?"

Marc-Olivier, who was at the next computer supposedly doing his geography project, turned around. "It's basically all of them, yes."

Maria typed her program anyway, the part she did understand. It asked for a number, stored it in n, and then did nothing useful with it. She stared at the screen. Somewhere in there, the computer would have to try dividing n by smaller numbers and find out whether any division came out even. But division in Python gave her answers like 2.571428571428571, and she did not want to compare a long ugly decimal against every possible even result. That way, she was fairly sure, lay madness.

She tried it with 18 divided by 7, and got 2.5714285714285714. Then she typed 18 divided by 6 and got 3.0, which was better but still awkward. What she wanted was a way to ask a yes-or-no question: did it divide evenly, or not? She scrolled through the notes Ms. Krause had photocopied for the club, and there it was, one line about the % operator. She typed 18 % 6 and the screen said 0. She typed 18 % 7 and the screen said 4.

"Okay," she said slowly. "The percent sign gives you the remainder. So n % d equals zero exactly when d divides n evenly. No remainder, no leftover piece. That's the whole question, answered." Her reasoning felt almost too simple, so she tested it. 20 % 5 was 0. 20 % 3 was 2. 13 % 2 was 1, 13 % 3 was 1, 13 % 4 was 1, and every one of those little leftover 1s was the program saying no, not this one. A prime would get no after no after no, all the way down. It was a pattern you could not see in the number itself, only in its remainders.

She wrote the loop, ran the program, and typed in 17. Prime, said the screen. She typed 18. Not prime. She typed 91, feeling clever, and the screen said not prime, which startled her until she checked and found 7 times 13. "Huh," she said. "It caught me."

Jet leaned over. "So is it done?"

"One more test." Maria typed 2, the smallest prime, and the tiniest edge case she could think of, the one she suspected would be inevitable trouble.

The screen said not prime. Maria put her forehead down on the keyboard for a moment, then sat up and started rereading her loop.

"That," said Marc-Olivier, "is why you test things."

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: A cast saw's blade vibrates rapidly back and forth instead of spinning, which lets it cut hard plaster or fiberglass without cutting the skin underneath.
story:
Friday's cast removal had felt inevitable ever since Dr. Patel said the words, and Alexandre had been dreading it for six weeks. He sat at the kitchen table with his encased arm propped on a pillow, watching a video on his mom's tablet for the fourth time. In the video, a cast saw shrieked through fiberglass and spat white dust everywhere. Cynthia arrived carrying a soccer sign-up sheet and her history textbook, because tryouts were Saturday and her project on the French monarchy was due Monday, and she had decided both problems could be solved at Alexandre's kitchen table.

"You're goalie or we don't have a team," she said, sliding the sheet toward him. "So stop watching that and watch this instead." She queued up a different video, one a girl had filmed in a hospital. In it, a boy yanked his arm away as the saw came near, and the nurse laughed kindly and said, "It vibrates back and forth instead of spinning. That's how it cuts the hard plaster and fiberglass without cutting the skin underneath." Alexandre rewound it twice. He had pictured a spinning blade, like a circular saw, and a spinning blade would go through skin the way it went through everything.

"So the blade isn't sharp sharp," Cynthia said slowly. "It just moves really fast sideways." Alexandre got up and fetched his mom's electric toothbrush. He held the humming head against the palm of his good hand and his skin wobbled like pudding, but nothing stung, nothing cut. Then he pressed it against his cast and the hard shell just buzzed. "To illustrate," he said, grabbing Cynthia's forearm and wiggling his fingertips back and forth on it as fast as he could. She laughed. "That tickles. It doesn't hurt at all."

They were still testing when Mr. Ricci knocked, returning the ladder he'd borrowed. When they told him why the toothbrush was out, he held up his own wrist. "Broke this in '09," he said. He went home and came back with a shoebox, and inside, folded open in two halves, sat his old cast, kept for a bet with his brother. Alexandre turned it over. The cut edges were clean through the shell, and the padding inside was untouched. "Never felt a thing," Mr. Ricci said. "Fell asleep once."

On Friday, when the nurse approached with the saw, Alexandre didn't pull away. He held out his arm, and the noise was as awful as the video, but he watched the dust fly and felt only a warm, buzzing tickle while the cast opened like a shell. Through the door, Cynthia held up the sign-up sheet and grinned. "Goalkeeper," she said.

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: A greenstick fracture is a break where the bone cracks on one side and bends on the other, like a young green branch; it happens mostly in children because their bones are more flexible.
story:
Emilia sat on the low concrete wall at the edge of the skate park, her right arm resting in a cast on her lap, and watched Blake carve back and forth across the shallow bowl. The morning was warm and the ramps smelled like sun-baked dust. She had been coming here every Saturday for a year, and this was the first one she had spent sitting still.

"Your turn," Blake called, rolling to a stop in front of her.

"Can't. Cast, remember?" She lifted her arm as proof, though the hard white shell was impossible to miss.

Blake dropped onto the wall beside her. "Steve said you told him your arm is only partly broken. That's not a thing, right? A bone's either broken or it isn't."

"It's a thing," Emilia said. "The doctor called it a greenstick fracture. The bone cracks on one side and bends on the other, like a young green branch. It happens mostly in kids because our bones are more flexible."

Blake frowned at her cast as if it might argue. "So part of your bone is just bent?"

"That's what I keep wondering about." Emilia turned her arm over. "You can't see through the cast. You can't feel the bone. For all I know, the crack side has already fixed itself and only the bend is left, or the whole thing is worse, or none of it is real and the doctor made it up. I can't check anything directly."

"So how would you check it?" Blake asked. "You'd need X-ray eyes."

"I don't need X-ray eyes. I need one fair test." She stood up, walked to the fence, and picked up a thin green twig that had blown down from the shade tree by the parking lot. She held it up. "If the bone really works like this, then this should work like the bone."

She pressed the twig against the wall and pushed. It bent, cracked along one side, and folded, still joined on the other. There it was, the exact shape the doctor had described, small and green and honest.

"Now the second part," she said. She splinted the twig against a straight stick with two rubber bands, the way her cast held her arm, and set it on the wall in the sun. "If it heals joined and straight, that's the pattern. Bones and branches, same rule."

"You're going to babysit a stick," Blake said.

"I'm going to nurture an experiment," Emilia said. "There's a difference, and it's not subjective."

They spent the rest of the morning taking turns on the flat ground, Blake pushing slowly so Emilia could practice balancing on the board with one good arm. Every so often she walked over and studied the twig on the wall.

When her mother picked her up that evening, Emilia carried the splinted twig carefully in her left hand. In the car, her phone buzzed. It was a text from Steve: asked the doctor again today for my own arm. Greenstick fracture. Same as yours. She looked at her twig, then out the window at the skate park shrinking behind them.

"Two for two," she said.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: Most vegetable seeds need water, oxygen and warmth to germinate, but not light; a few, such as lettuce, sprout better with light and are sown very shallowly.
story:
Katherine pressed her thumb into the soil of plot fourteen and dropped in another lettuce seed, this time barely covering it with dust. The whole row had been planted two weeks ago, deep and neat, and not one green speck had come up. Down the path, Theodor's carrots were already showing their feathery little tops, and Myah's beans had fat green hooks pushing out of the ground.

"Maybe your seeds were bad," Myah said, kneeling beside her with a watering can.

"They can't all be bad." Katherine turned the seed packet over and read it again. Sow shallowly, it said, in small print she had skipped the first time. Press into surface. She had dug those seeds in a knuckle deep, the way the beans wanted. Theodor wandered over from his carrots, wiping dirt on his knees, and looked at the empty row.

"Your beans came up underground," he said. "So seeds don't need light to sprout. But maybe lettuce is different. Maybe lettuce is one that does."

Katherine thought about that all through lunch, sitting on the fence rail beside the old electric fence box with its warning sticker about high voltage. Most of the seeds had come up in the dark, under the soil. Warmth, water, and air were what they needed, and the ground had all three. But the packet had said shallowly, and that made sense only if the lettuce seeds needed light itself. The seed packet was an eccentric old thing, printed in tiny type, but it was telling her something.

She went back and ran a test. Half the row she left as a mistake, seeds still buried deep. The other half she resowed, scattering seed on top of the damp soil and pressing each one down so it sat barely covered, where light could reach it. She watered both halves the same, and she covered neither, and she wrote it all in her notebook in careful columns so she could compare.

Four days later she was at the gate before anyone else, Myah jogging up the lane behind her with two granola bars because Katherine always forgot to eat when she was excited. The shallow half of the row had sprouted, dozens of pale green pinpricks in a line, while the deep half showed nothing at all. Katherine crouched there so long her knees ached.

When Ms. Halvorsen came by with the community garden clipboard, Katherine showed her the notebook, both columns, the dates, the difference between the two halves. "I want to advocate for a sign at the seed table," she said. "So nobody else buries their lettuce. Beans and carrots can sprout in the dark, but lettuce wants light, so it goes in shallow." Ms. Halvorsen read the columns twice, then said the garden had a spare board and some paint in the shed.

They made the sign that afternoon, Theodor lettering LETTUCE GOES LIGHTLY while Myah painted a fat green sprout at the top. Katherine planted a second bed of lettuce along the fence, each seed pressed just under the surface, and stood back to look at the row. "Grow fast," she told it. "I'll be back tomorrow."

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: A red herring is a false clue placed on purpose to lead readers toward the wrong conclusion, so not every hint in a story is real foreshadowing.
story:
Riley arrived at the bookshop ten minutes early, which gave him time to buy two cookies instead of one and to feel smug about it. The book club met in the back corner, between the poetry shelf and a cardboard cutout of a detective holding a magnifying glass. Leopold was already there, tapping the week's short story against the table like a judge with a gavel.

"She's the murderer," Leopold announced before Riley sat down. "Page three, she wears green gloves. Green gloves! In the last scene, the thief leaves a green thread on the windowsill. That's foreshadowing, obviously."

Henrik slid his copy across the table. "But she also says she hates the victim in paragraph one. That's so obvious it's almost boring. I don't trust it."

"You don't trust foreshadowing?" Leopold said. "It's a literary technique. My sister taught me that on Tuesday."

Riley chewed his cookie and flipped to page three. The green gloves were there, sure enough, mentioned twice, almost like the author was nudging them with an elbow. Twice seemed like a lot of nudging. He thought about their class lesson, where Ms. Thompson had written HINTS on the board and circled it, and how she'd said some hints were honest and some were, in her words, sneaky. He couldn't remember the sneaky kind's name, but he remembered the shape of the idea: an author could plant a clue just to send you galloping off in the wrong direction, the way a false trail leads hunting dogs astray.

"Hold on," Riley said. He reread the last page. "Look at the gardener. He appears in exactly one sentence, fixing the hedge under the window. The window with the thread. Why fix a hedge in the rain?"

"Because he's a gardener," Leopold said. "Gardeners garden. It's practically their whole deal."

But Riley had started dismantling Leopold's theory piece by piece, laying each clue on the table like evidence. The green gloves, the loud public grudge, the dramatic page-three promise to get revenge, all of it too bright, too visible, like a decoy flare. He checked the copyright page and found the story was from a mystery anthology. Mystery writers played tricks. That was the whole sport.

"I think the green thread is a trap," Riley said. "There's a word for it. A red herring. A false clue put there on purpose so readers leap to the wrong ending."

The shop bell jingled, and Ms. Thompson herself came around the poetry shelf, holding a stack of books she wasn't even buying. She raised an eyebrow at their argument, and Riley explained both theories: the explicit green-glove chain versus his one quiet gardener in the rain. She smiled in a way that gave away nothing, which Riley felt was its own kind of hint.

They voted. Henrik sided with Riley, Leopold grumbled about democracy, and they read the final page aloud together. The gardener had done it. Leopold stared at his copy like it had personally betrayed him, then laughed so hard he knocked over the cardboard detective.

"Fine," Leopold said, standing the detective back up. "But next week, I'm finding the red herring before either of you."

"Next week," Riley said, "I'm bringing three cookies."

activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
knowledge_domain: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
fact: Lifting the lid while rice simmers lets steam escape, which can leave the grains undercooked.
story:
Mia stood in the kitchen with three things going at once: a pot of rice, a pan of curry bubbling at the corner of the stove, and a circle of flatbread dough warming on the griddle. Her plan was sketched on paper, a little chart to depict the order of everything, rice first because it took longest, curry next, flatbread last. On the counter beside the chart sat a note in her mom's handwriting, sparse and to the point: "Back at 7. Dinner is yours tonight. Love, Mom." That was the deal. Mia had promised a full meal, all three parts ready together, and she intended to keep it.

The problem was the rice. She had set the timer for eighteen minutes, but every few minutes she lifted the lid to check. The grains looked the same each time, pale and sitting in their water, so she peeked again sooner, sure that watching would help. "It's not doing anything," she muttered, and lifted the lid once more.

Her phone buzzed. It was a message from Hareem: "How's the big dinner? Surviving?" Mia typed back with flour on her thumb: "Rice is suspicious. It just sits there." Hareem replied with a single wide-eyed emoji and the words, "My gran says leave the pot alone. She yells at me for peeking." Then a second message: "Something about the steam. Ask Caelan, he cooks."

Mia set the phone down and stared at the pot. Steam. Every time she lifted the lid, that white cloud rolled out and vanished, and she had never once thought about where it was going. She tried an experiment. She replaced the lid, folded a dish towel over the rim, and made herself walk away. She rolled out the next flatbread, flipped the one on the griddle, stirred the curry until its surface went glossy. The kitchen smelled like onions and cumin and hot bread. The suspense of not looking was almost worse than the cooking itself, but she kept her hands busy and her eyes on everything except that pot.

When the timer finally rang, she lifted the lid once, all the way, and there it was: the water gone, the grains plump and steaming in soft little rows. She tested a spoonful against the roof of her mouth. Tender, all the way through. Her earlier peeks had let steam escape and the last batch she had made this way had come out crunchy in the middle, and now she understood why without anyone having to tell her. She piled the flatbreads into a towel to stay warm and carried the pot to the table just as the front door opened.

Her mom came in with her coat still on and stopped at the smell of it. "You did all three?" she said, dropping her bag. Mia grinned and lifted the lid of the curry one last time, letting the steam curl up between them. "Everything's hot at the same time," she said. "Sit down before the bread gets cold."

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Thailand, the head is considered sacred, so touching someone's head, even to pat a child, can be seen as rude.
story:
Aaron had exactly nine dollars and a plan: buy a gift at the cultural festival for his grandmother, who was coming to visit on Sunday, and who always said that a gift chosen by hand meant more than one chosen by a phone. He also wanted to try the mango sticky rice, but the gift came first, so he kept the money zipped in his pocket and walked past the food stalls with the stiff dignity of a boy ignoring a siren.

He found Andie at the Thai community booth, where her aunt was arranging little carved elephants on a cloth. Andie waved him over. A younger boy, maybe six, was weaving between the tables with a paper lantern, and he was about to be very annoying, so Aaron reached out to ruffle his hair the way his uncle always ruffled his.

"Don't," Andie said, grabbing his wrist. "In Thailand the head is sacred. Touching someone's head, even just to pat a kid, can be seen as rude."

Aaron lowered his hand. The little boy spun past, oblivious, his lantern squeaking. "Good thing you caught me," Aaron said. "That would have been a great way to start a friendship."

Andie's aunt handed each of them a small dish of sticky rice with a fork. Aaron noticed that Andie held the fork in her left hand and pushed food onto it with a spoon, so he copied her, badly, dropping a grain of rice onto his shoe. He also noticed something else. Twice, when customers reached over the elephants, the aunt gave a small bow with her palms together, and twice, they bowed back, confused but game. Aaron made an inference: the bow was not just hello, it was also a graceful way of saying watch where your hands go.

He tested it. When a man leaned across the cloth to point at an elephant with one finger, Aaron caught Andie's eye and put his palms together. She grinned and bowed at the man, who straightened up immediately, apologizing to the whole table.

For his grandmother, Aaron chose a painted elephant, then thought of the little boy with the lantern and bought a second, smaller one, which he concealed in his backpack in case the moment for giving it never came. He didn't want a scene. At the edge of the booth, the boy was sulking because his lantern had torn on a tent stake.

"Excuse me," Aaron said, palms together, and offered the elephant with both hands, the way he had watched the aunt hand over change. The boy snatched it and ran off without bowing. "You're welcome," Aaron said.

"Your bow was lopsided," Andie said.

"It's not hereditary, I have to practice." He bowed again, deeper this time, and somewhere behind him, her aunt laughed and bowed back.

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms became part of Canada's Constitution when it was proclaimed on April 17, 1982.
story:
The assignment was due first period tomorrow, and Marcus still did not have it done. Ms. Perera had given the class three days to pick one right from the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, read it carefully, and explain it in their own words to a small group. He had put it off, and now it was 7:40 in the evening and his notebook had one sentence in it: "freedom of thought maybe."

He biked to the school anyway, because Ms. Perera had said the lobby would be open for the community legal clinic that ran on Thursdays. She had also taped a full copy of the Charter to the wall outside the office, the same one that hung in courthouses across the country. Marcus stood in front of it with his notebook open. At the bottom, in small print, was a date: the Charter had become part of Canada's Constitution when it was proclaimed on April 17, 1982.

That date irritated him, the way a pebble in a shoe does. "Wait," he said to the janitor buffing the floor. "If the Charter only became part of the Constitution in 1982, what were people's rights before that? Did they have none?" The janitor shrugged and kept buffing. Marcus decided to test it. His grandfather always said Canada had a Constitution long before he was born, so maybe the Constitution existed first and the Charter was added to it later, like a new wing on an old school. If that was true, then 1982 was the moment the Charter joined, not the moment rights began.

He wrote that down as a question to check, then went back to the poster and read Section 2 over and over until the words stopped sliding around. Everyone had the freedom of thought, belief, opinion, and expression, including freedom of the press. He tried saying it to himself without the poster: you can believe what you believe, and you can say it, and reporters can print it, and the government cannot just shut that down. When he wrote it that way, it sounded like something a person would actually fight for.

In the morning he found Isaak and Delaney at the lab table and laid out his pages. "I picked freedom of expression," he said. "You can hold an opinion and say it out loud without the government stopping you. Newspapers get it too, which is why a free press can be so influential, it can change what a whole country thinks." Delaney frowned at his last page. "What's this question about 1982?"

"That's the part I figured out. The Charter became part of Canada's Constitution when it was proclaimed on April 17, 1982. My grandpa confirmed it on the phone last night." He tapped the page. "Before that, the Constitution was already there, but the Charter wasn't part of it yet. Like the school was built first and the new gym came later."

"Okay, show-off," Isaak said, pulling his own crumpled pages from his backpack, "but if you're done, help me, because I picked the right against unreasonable search and I don't even know what unreasonable means."

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: Gold was discovered at Sutter's Mill in California in January 1848, starting the California Gold Rush that drew people west in huge numbers.
story:
Camille leaned over the glass case at the historic site, her nose almost touching it. Inside lay a settler's diary, opened to a page from 1849, the ink faded to brown. Her worksheet had one question on it: use a primary source to explain why people moved west in the 1800s. The problem was that the diary's handwriting looped and shrank until some words looked like knots of thread.

"I can read three words," she whispered to Brendan, who was crouched beside her. "River. Fever. And I think that one says Sacramento."

Brendan wanted to find something about farms. He had bet Nassim two cookies that most settlers came west for land, and he needed proof before lunch. "Look for the word acres," he said, running his finger above the glass without touching it. "Diaries always talk about acres."

Camille squinted at a smudged line. "Here's fever again. Gold fever." She read it twice, the second time louder. "He wrote it twice in one paragraph. Why would a farmer write about a fever?"

"Because people got sick on the trail," Brendan said. "My uncle says half of them nearly died of fatigue before they even crossed the mountains."

Camille ignored that. She was chasing something she couldn't see yet, an idea hiding under the ink. Farmers wrote about soil and rain. This man wrote about gold, and Sacramento, and a place he called the mill. She flipped her worksheet over and copied the diary line word for word, loops and all, then counted the other pages the guide had photographed and posted on the wall. Page after page, the same fever.

"Wait," Brendan said, standing up so fast his chair scraped. "If everyone's got gold fever, maybe they're not coming for farms at all. Maybe they're coming for the money."

Camille grabbed his arm. "Nassim!" she called across the room. "Come look at this!"

Nassim trotted over, still holding the two cookies he hoped to keep. Camille pointed at the wall display, at a printed timeline next to the photographs. "Gold was discovered at Sutter's Mill in California in January 1848," she read. "That's before this diary. That's why everyone's rushing." She looked from the timeline to the glass case and back. "It started the Gold Rush. It drew people west in huge numbers."

Brendan groaned and handed over the cookies. "Some of them probably still wanted farms," he said, but Camille was already writing, filling the back of her worksheet with the settler's own words about fever and the mill, proof straight from the source. She waved the page at Ms. Chanthavong, who was helping another group across the room.

"Ms. Chanthavong!" Camille called. "Can I read this out loud?"

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: A stuffy nose during a cold is caused mainly by swollen blood vessels and inflamed tissue in the lining of the nose, not only by a buildup of mucus.
story:
Xavier sat on the edge of his bed surrounded by a fortress of crumpled tissues, and he blew his nose again just to hear the same disappointing result: nothing. The blockage was still there, solid as a wall. He had spent all of Tuesday believing that if he just kept blowing, the stuffiness would empty out like a sink draining. It had not worked. His wastebasket was overflowing, his nose was raw, and the wall remained.

He picked up his phone and typed a message to Marwa, who had been home sick the week before him. "Did your nose ever actually unstuff? I've blown mine like forty times. Nothing comes out."

Her reply came fast. "Same. I kept blowing until my mom took the whole tissue box away."

Xavier frowned at the screen. That was strange. If a stuffy nose were only mucus, blowing should fix it. Marwa had produced nothing, and he was producing nothing, yet both of them had felt like their noses were packed shut. He tried to quantify it, counting in his head: he had blown his nose eleven times since breakfast, and the blocked feeling had not changed even once. Eleven tries, zero improvement. That was a pattern, and patterns meant something hidden was going on.

He searched his symptoms on his laptop, scrolling past an eccentric site that claimed colds could be cured with hot sauce and a headstand, and found a plain medical page. He read the sentence twice, then read it out loud to the empty bedroom. "A stuffy nose during a cold is caused mainly by swollen blood vessels and inflamed tissue in the lining of the nose, not only by a buildup of mucus." So it was swelling inside, not snot. He had been attacking the wrong thing all day. No wonder the wall would not drain. He thought guiltily of Sunday, when he had skipped washing his hands at Marwa's birthday lunch because the line for the bathroom was long and the cuisine, her grandmother's soup, was too good to wait for. Maybe the cold had come from that choice, or maybe from the doorknob at school, or from Jonathan's sneeze in science class. He would never know, and that bothered him more than the stuffiness did.

He texted Marwa the sentence, then added, "So blowing harder is pointless. We've basically been trying to empty a nose that isn't full."

There was a long pause, then typing bubbles, then: "You're telling me I sacrificed a whole tissue box for nothing?"

"For swelling," Xavier typed. "Steam's supposed to help. I'm going to try a hot shower and stop blowing unless something's actually coming out." He felt almost cheerful about surrendering, which was a strange thing to feel while still sick.

Twenty minutes later, wrapped in his towel with his nose clearer than it had been all day, he took a photo of the wastebasket and sent it to Marwa with one line: "In memoriam. Forty tissues, zero snot."

Her answer made him laugh out loud. "Light a candle for them. Also, if you ever see me near a tissue box again, take it away."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The first Super Bowl's official name was the AFL-NFL World Championship Game; the Roman numeral 'Super Bowl I' was added later.
story:
The living room smelled like melted cheese and burnt popcorn. Alexis sat on the floor between Dean and Maxime, holding the remote because her dad had put her in charge of the sound. On the screen, two teams ran onto the field under bright lights while the announcers talked over the crowd noise.

"Why does it say Roman numerals after the name?" Dean asked, pointing at the corner of the screen. "Like, why not just the year?"

"Probably so old games and new games don't get mixed up," Maxime said, chewing.

Alexis thought about that. It sounded right, but something bothered her. "Wait. If the numbers were always there, then the first one would have been called Super Bowl I, right? Before the second game even happened." She frowned. "Who names something number one when there's only one of it and nobody knows there'll be more?"

"So your premise is that the numbering started later," Maxime said.

"Yeah. And I can check." Ms. Singh, their neighbor from across the hall, had knocked twenty minutes ago carrying a bowl of samosas to accompany the chips, and she'd stayed for the kickoff. She was old enough to have watched a lot of football. Alexis turned around. "Ms. Singh, the very first big game. What was it called?"

Ms. Singh laughed. "Everybody gets that wrong. It was called the AFL-NFL World Championship Game."

Dean set down his drink. "That's it? No Super Bowl at all?"

"No Roman numeral either, not then. The numeral came along afterward," Ms. Singh said. "Look it up if you don't believe me."

Alexis grabbed her dad's tablet from the end table and typed. The results loaded slow because everyone's phones were on the wifi. She scrolled, read, and then held the screen up so Dean and Maxime could see it. "She's right. The name came later. So the first game never got called Super Bowl I until people went back and numbered it."

"Ms. Singh wins," Maxime said, and passed her the samosas first.

At halftime, Alexis's grandmother, who watched the game from the armchair and mostly ignored the kids, tapped Alexis on the shoulder. "Your aunt texted me to ask the score," she said, holding out her phone. "Tell her."

Alexis typed the score, then added one more line: Fun fact, the first one was officially the AFL-NFL World Championship Game. The Roman numerals got added later. She hit send and set the phone on the carpet.

Her grandmother's phone buzzed before the second half started. "She says, 'I did not know that.'"

"Nobody does," Dean said. "That's the whole point."

The whistle blew. On the screen, the returner caught the ball at the five, and Alexis turned the volume up.

activity: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
knowledge_domain: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
fact: A first thesis is often called a working thesis because it can change; if the evidence points somewhere else, a careful writer revises the thesis instead of ignoring the evidence.
story:
Eella tapped her pencil against the library table until Piper reached over and laid a hand flat on it, gently, like she was calming a hummingbird. The assignment sheet from Ms. Tesfaye sat between them: a persuasive essay, five paragraphs, with the thesis and three-point outline due Thursday. Ella had chosen her topic on Monday with total confidence. The school should ban vending machines, because they made students unhealthy, wasted money, and ruined lunchtime appetites. Three points. Done.

"It's perfect," she had told Piper then. "I just have to find quotes that prove it."

Now it was Wednesday afternoon, and the library was tranquil except for the soft clatter of the keyboard in the corner. Ella had three articles open on the laptop, and every one of them had betrayed her. The first said students at schools with vending machines that stocked juice and granola actually ate slightly better snacks. The second said the machines raised money for the band and the soccer team. Ella winced when she found the third, a survey showing most students bought snacks after school, not before lunch.

"None of it proves my points," she said. "It kind of proves the opposite."

Piper leaned over and read the screen. "So find better articles."

"There aren't better articles. There's just these." Ella scrolled back to the top, looking for something she might have missed. Then she stared at her outline, the three neat points with nothing under them but empty brackets where quotes were supposed to go. It was like watching a magician's trick backwards. The evidence was the signal, and it was pointing somewhere she hadn't planned to go.

She opened a new page in her notebook and tried a sentence she didn't like: Schools should keep vending machines but require healthier options. She read it aloud in a mutter. Piper raised an eyebrow. Ella wrote it again, tighter. Schools should keep vending machines and stock them with healthier choices, because machines can fund teams, students snack after school anyway, and better options improve what students eat. Her three old points, flipped and rebuilt, stood underneath like scaffolding.

Ella found Ms. Tesfaye by the printer and handed over both pages, the old outline and the new one. Ms. Tesfaye read the first, then the second, and smiled. "You learned what a working thesis is for," she said. "It works until the evidence turns you around."

Ella went back to the table, and Piper slid the laptop across. "Quotes for point one?"

"Quotes for point one," Ella said, and picked up her pencil.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: A layer of mulch, such as straw or wood chips, keeps soil moist, blocks weeds from sprouting and evens out soil temperature.
story:
Lincoln pressed his thumb into the soil of bed number nine and grinned. Damp. He pressed his thumb into bed number ten, right beside it, and the crust cracked like a stale cookie. Same sun, same rain, same morning. He crouched there in the community garden with dirt on his knees, staring at the two beds like they were a magic trick he had to figure out.

The difference wasn't a mystery for long, because it was lying right on top of bed nine: a thick blanket of straw that old Mr. Harper had spread there in June. Bed ten was Lincoln's own, bare and proud, and every seedling he'd planted in it was small, pale, and vulnerable, drooping by noon no matter how much he watered. Bed nine, which belonged to Mr. Harper, had tomato plants so thick with leaves they looked like shrubs.

"You're watering twice as much as me," Lincoln said to Mr. Harper over the fence between the plots. "I've watched you. Once a week, maybe."

"Once a week," Mr. Harper agreed, pulling a weed that had dared to sprout at the edge of the straw. "Your bed's a battlefield, son. Weeds invade any patch of naked dirt. Mine can't get through the straw."

Lincoln dragged a fingertip along the top of the straw. Underneath, the soil was cool and dark. Under his own crust, the dirt in bed ten felt like it had been baked. His seedlings were thirsty in the morning and cooked by afternoon, while Mr. Harper's tomatoes sat in dirt that stayed the same temperature day after day.

That night, Lincoln looked up straw on his mom's laptop and found a word: mulch. A layer of mulch, like straw or wood chips, keeps soil moist, blocks weeds from sprouting, and evens out soil temperature. He read the line twice, then jumped up so fast his chair squeaked. That was it. That was the whole difference between bed nine and bed ten, and he could copy it.

The next morning he rode his bike to the garden supply store with birthday money jingling in his pocket, worried the whole way that wood chips would cost more than a mortgage payment. The cashier laughed at that. "A bale of straw, kid. Five dollars." Five dollars! He bought two, because he was not taking chances.

Kinley and Hugo met him at the garden, and the three of them spread straw around every seedling in bed ten, tucking it in close but not touching the stems. "This is going to work," Hugo kept saying, patting the straw flat. "Watch, by August we're going to have a jungle." Kinley took a before photo of the cracked dirt with her phone so they could compare.

A week later Lincoln knelt at the edge of his bed and slid his hand under the straw. Cool. Damp. Dark. Beside the fence, only three little weeds had poked up where the straw was thin, instead of the dozens that used to crowd every corner. He yanked those three and held them up like trophies.

"Kinley! Hugo! Come feel this!"

They came running, and all three of them stood there with their hands buried in the straw, grinning at each other.

"Now the jungle part," Hugo said.

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Phishing is a scam in which someone pretends to be a trusted company or person to trick you into giving away passwords or other private information.
story:
Victoria had wanted a phone for exactly two years, and on Saturday morning the box was finally on the kitchen table. Her mom set down one rule before handing it over: the phone came with responsibilities, and if anything on it felt strange, Victoria had to show her. Victoria agreed, mostly to get the box open faster.

By afternoon she had downloaded her favourite game, Dragon Reach, and messaged Keon three times about it. Then a text arrived. "WARNING: Your Dragon Reach account will be deleted in 24 hours unless you verify your password. Reply now." Her stomach dropped. She had spent a whole year earning her dragon collection. Her thumb hovered over the reply box. She typed her password, then stopped. Why would the game need her password? It already knew her password. That was the whole point of a password. She deleted the message, dragged her desk chair to the window to think, and watched the rain start, a thin precipitation streaking the glass. Nothing in the sky told you where the wind came from. You had to test it. Well, she could test this too. If the warning were real, the game itself would say so.

She opened Dragon Reach. Her account was fine. No warning banner, no deletion notice, nothing. She checked the sender's number, which was a random pile of digits, and a tiny seed of an idea sprouted: somebody was pretending to be the game so she would hand over her password. She texted Mercedes, whose older brother had lost his account last year. Mercedes replied fast: "That's phishing. Someone pretends to be a trusted company or person to trick you into giving away passwords or private info. My brother replied to one and lost everything." Victoria read it twice, then blocked the number. It was a small move against somebody invisible, and it felt good anyway, like locking a door behind her.

On Monday she told Ms. Katz about it, expecting maybe a lecture, but Ms. Katz only asked whether Victoria had replied with any part of her password. She hadn't. "Then you did exactly right," Ms. Katz said. "Some adults don't manage that." Victoria felt less frail about the whole thing, less like the phone was a machine built to intimidate her.

At home she showed her mom the blocked number and the saved screenshot. Her mom looked it over and nodded slowly. "Okay," she said. "You can keep the phone." Victoria set it on the counter beside the dragon-shaped lamp Keon had given her for her birthday, and texted him one line: "Account safe. Dragon lives."

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: The equals sign was invented by the Welsh mathematician Robert Recorde in 1557, who chose two parallel lines because no two things could be more equal.
story:
The problem on the board was x + 7 = 19, and Ms. Esposito had drawn a seesaw under it, which Leah found insulting. She was eleven. She had seen a seesaw before. What she had not seen was why subtracting seven from both sides was legal, and the seesaw did not answer that, because seesaws were for kindergartners and for cargo nets full of sandbags, which was what Ms. Esposito compared the equation to next. "Picture x as a mystery box of cargo," she said, "and seven bricks on the other side."

Leah wrote the problem in her notebook and then wrote it again, because something bothered her about the equals sign itself. Two little lines, sitting there like train tracks. She raised her hand. "Who decided it looks like that? Why not a squiggle?"

Ms. Esposito smiled the way teachers do when they have been waiting all year for someone to ask. "Look it up tonight and tell us tomorrow."

Leah forgot until she was at her grandmother's kitchen table, the notebook still luminous under the lamp, the equation still unsolved. She looked it up. The equals sign was invented by a Welsh mathematician named Robert Recorde in 1557. He chose two parallel lines because, he said, no two things could be more equal.

She sat with that for a while. Not a squiggle. Not an arrow. Two lines exactly the same length, exactly parallel, like they would go on forever without ever touching or drifting apart. It was not a command, like she had thought. It was a promise. Whatever sat on the left would always match whatever sat on the right.

So she tested it. If the two sides were truly equal, then doing the same thing to both should keep them equal. She took x + 7 = 19 and subtracted seven from the left side. Then, holding her breath a little, she subtracted seven from the right side too. x = 12. She checked it backward: 12 plus 7 was 19. The train tracks still matched. She tried another, 3x = 15, and divided both sides by 3. x = 5. It worked again. It was not a trick Ms. Esposito had made up. It was a rule she could classify under things that were actually true, unlike the rumor about the cafeteria meatloaf.

The next morning she told the class about Robert Recorde and the parallel lines, and Ciara said, "So the equals sign is basically a really old promise," and Maika said, "A 1557 promise," which Leah felt covered it.

At lunch, Ciara slid her own worksheet across the table. "I got x = 40 on this one but the answer key says x = 4. What did I do wrong?"

Leah looked at 8x = 32, then at Ciara's work, where she had multiplied both sides by 8 instead of dividing.

"You broke the promise," Leah said, and took the pencil.

activity: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
knowledge_domain: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
fact: If a wire has 6 volts across it and 2 amps flowing through it, its resistance is 6 divided by 2, which is 3 ohms.
story:
Megan squinted at the multimeter and wrote down her numbers: 6 volts across the wire, 2 amps flowing through it. Across the lab bench, Carter was already punching his calculator like it owed him money.

"I got twelve," Carter announced. "I multiplied six by two. Twelve ohms."

"Twelve ohms seems huge for one little wire," Megan said. Faith leaned over from the next bench, where she was supposed to be recording data on a cargo shipment simulation for Mr. Müller's other class, but the electricity station was clearly more interesting. The three of them stared at the wire, which lay there being thin and ordinary and refusing to reveal anything.

Megan thought back to the week before, when the class had done the boat experiment. Twelve grams of clay had sunk instantly, and she had been sure the clay was the problem until Faith suggested testing the shape instead of the material. They had folded the same clay into a bowl, and it had floated. The lesson had stuck with her: when a number looks wrong, test the rule, not just the material. "Let's try division instead," she said now. "Six divided by two. That's three."

"Three ohms," Faith read over her shoulder. Carter frowned at his calculator, cleared it, and tried again. Three. Megan advocated for one more test before they told Mr. Müller anything, because a single measurement wasn't authentic data, as he liked to say; it was a guess with a decimal point. They swapped in a different spool of wire, measured again, and wrote the new numbers in Carter's careful handwriting. When they compared results with another group across the room, whose answer also came out small and sensible, Carter actually grinned.

Mr. Müller stopped at their bench on his rounds and looked at the page. "So what is the resistance of that wire?" he asked.

"Three ohms," Megan said, and turned the notebook so he could see the numbers for himself.

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: Babies under one year should be put to sleep on their backs, on a firm, flat surface with no pillows, blankets or toys, which lowers the risk of sudden infant death.
story:
The note from Ms. Clarke was stuck to the fridge with a magnet shaped like a lemon, and Maya had read it four times already. "Omar naps around 7:30. Back to sleep, firm flat mattress, nothing in the crib. No pillows, no blankets, no toys. My number is below." Omar was eight months old, and Maya was babysitting him alone for the first time, which was why Eshaal was on the couch texting her encouragement.

"Did you know," Eshaal wrote, "that when my mom's corporation did that charity drive, everyone voted unanimous to donate cribs? Newborn stuff. It was a whole meeting." Maya smiled at her phone, then looked over at the portable crib Ms. Clarke had set up in the kitchen. The mattress was thin and hard, like something you would not choose for yourself, and the sheet was pulled tight. Around it sat a basket of soft things: a fleecy blanket with bears on it, a small pillow, a stuffed rabbit with one ear.

At 7:25 Omar rubbed his eyes and fussed, so Maya lifted him, warmed his bottle, and paced the kitchen floor with him until his fist went slack against her shoulder. When she carried him to the crib, she saw the fleece blanket draped over the rail, right where a tired person would grab it. Her hand was already reaching for it when she remembered the note, and before that, remembered something older.

Last spring, before her mom would let her enroll in the babysitting course at the community center, Maya had watched a video there with the other kids. A nurse had placed a doll on its back on a bare mattress and said, "Babies under one go to sleep like this, on their backs, on a firm flat surface, with no pillows, blankets or toys, because it lowers the risk of sudden infant death." Maya had thought it looked almost too plain, a crib with nothing in it, like a room with the furniture taken out. She had written it down word for word in her notebook anyway.

Now she pulled the blanket, the pillow, and the rabbit off the rail and set them on the counter, out of reach. The mattress felt firm under her palm, and flat, just as the note said. She laid Omar down on his back, and his eyelids fluttered once and stayed shut. His arms rose up on either side of his head, like a tiny person surrendering to sleep.

She texted Eshaal: "He's down. Bare crib, on his back, like the video said. Blanket's on the counter." Eshaal sent back a row of stars. Maya sat where she could see the crib and the kitchen doorway both, and listened to the small, even sound of Omar breathing.

When Ms. Clarke came home at 9:40, she peeked into the crib first, before she even took off her coat. She looked at the empty mattress, then at the counter where the bears and the rabbit waited in a neat pile. "You put him on his back," she said. "Nothing in the crib."

"That's what the note said," Maya answered. Ms. Clarke set her keys down gently, as if the quiet itself were something not to be broken.

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: In the United States, the national Poison Help line is 1-800-222-1222, and it connects callers to a local poison control center at any hour.
story:
Aurora had assumed babysitting a two-year-old would be easy money, since Milo mostly stacked blocks and said "no" to everything. She'd been at the neighbor's house for forty minutes, texting Ophelia about the history homework, when the kitchen went quiet. Quiet was bad. She found Milo beside the sink with an open bottle of all-purpose cleaner in his fists, a puddle spreading across the tile.

Her first instinct was to call her mom, but her mom was at a movie and would panic before she helped. Then she remembered what Mr. Bautista, her gym teacher, had drilled into them last spring during a safety unit, the one day they'd practiced something instead of running laps. "Before you assume the worst," he'd said, "get the number that's already in the house." At the time she'd thought that was a weird thing to say, and she'd changed her mind about it right now, standing in a stranger's kitchen with her heart going like a drum.

She crouched down and pried the bottle out of Milo's sticky hands, holding it up to the light. The cap was off, but how much was gone? Half an inch? She couldn't tell, because she had no idea how full it had been. There was a beautiful symmetry to the problem: the thing she most needed to know was the one thing she couldn't see. Milo himself was the only witness, and his answer to "did you drink this?" was to laugh and say "ba."

Aurora set him on her hip, keeping his mouth away from her shoulder, and started opening drawers and cabinets. On the front of the fridge, half hidden under a crayon drawing of what looked like a purple dog, was a taped index card. Poison Help, it said, 1-800-222-1222. The card explained that the line connects you to your local poison control center, any hour of the day or night. She dialed with her thumb while Milo tried to eat the purple dog.

A calm woman answered before the second ring finished. Aurora described the cleaner, the open cap, and Milo's age, and admitted she didn't know how much was missing. The woman asked questions in a steady voice: was he coughing, was he drooling, did his mouth look red? No, no, and no. She told Aurora to give him water, watch him closely, and call back if anything changed. Then she asked one more question that cracked the case wide open. "Is the puddle sticky?"

Aurora touched the spill and her fingers came away tacky and sweet. She lifted the bottle to her nose and smelled fake grape, not chemicals. The cap Milo had opened was on a different bottle entirely, a refillable one the family used for bubble solution, sitting in the same spot under the sink where a careless hand had left it next to the cleaner. The cleaner bottle was still sealed. Milo had poured bubble soap on the floor and was extremely proud of it.

She mopped up the purple puddle while Milo supervised from his high chair, drinking his water like a tiny boss. When the parents came home, Aurora handed over the index card from the fridge and said, "You might want to move the bubble stuff."

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: An emergency dispatcher usually first asks for the address of the emergency, so a babysitter should know the exact address of the house they are in.
story:
Kayla wrote the address on a sticky note before the Winters even finished putting on their coats: 14 Maple Grove Road. She stuck it to the fridge right beside the phone, because she'd heard somewhere that if you ever had to call for help, the dispatcher would want the address first, before anything else.

"Very thorough," said Mrs. Winters, laughing. "He naps at two. We'll be back by four."

The moment the door clicked shut, Kayla stood in the quiet kitchen feeling like a real babysitter at last. Louis-Felix had texted her three times already, saying he was optimistic she'd get to babysit again, maybe even for his little cousin, if tonight went well. She checked on the baby, whose name was Theo, then settled on the couch to monitor him on the little camera screen. He slept. She grinned. This was easy.

At 3:40, Theo woke up crying, and then came the coughing. Not a normal cough. It came in tight, squeaky bursts, and his lips looked pale in the camera's gray light. Kayla's heart slammed, but her brain started working too. Theo had seemed fine all afternoon, so something had changed. She scanned the crib and spotted a small red wheel, half hidden under the blanket. A tiny toy car. He must have gotten hold of it, and now he couldn't catch his breath.

She scooped him up, and the wheel was not in his hand. It might still be in his mouth. "Okay," she said out loud. "Okay." She grabbed the phone, and her thumb hovered over the numbers while her mind went blank with panic. Then she saw the sticky note on the fridge, exactly where she'd put it. She dialed, and when the calm voice answered, she was ready for the very first question, because the dispatcher asked for the address of the emergency before anything else.

"Fourteen Maple Grove Road," Kayla said, steady and fast. She explained the wheel and the squeaky cough, and the dispatcher talked her through it while an ambulance rolled toward them. Kayla held Theo, tilted him forward the way the voice described, and prayed. Then something small and red dropped onto the kitchen floor and bounced once, and Theo gulped in a huge, ragged breath and started to wail, loud and furious and wonderful.

The paramedics arrived anyway, and the Winters came home early, and everyone said she'd done exactly right. Theo fell asleep on his mother's shoulder before they even left the kitchen. Kayla peeled the sticky note off the fridge and pressed it into her pocket, then texted Louis-Felix with shaking, delighted hands: "Babysitting again Saturday. Bringing my own sticky notes."

activity: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
knowledge_domain: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
fact: Street names are rarely used in Japanese addresses outside a few cities such as Kyoto, so people giving directions usually point to landmarks and train stations.
story:
Claire had practiced her one Japanese sentence all week, whispering it on the bus, in the shower, into her pillow until her little brother banged on the wall. Now, standing at the gate of the cultural festival with Caius and Angelique, she had a real reason to use it. The map in her hand showed that the calligraphy demonstration, the prestigious one with a visiting master from Osaka, was somewhere past the food stalls, but the dotted lines on the map made no sense at all.

"You go first," Angelique said, nudging her. "You're the one who studied."

Claire found a woman ladling soup behind a stall and took a breath. "Sumimasen," she said, and then, carefully, she asked for the street the demonstration was on. The woman smiled, nodded, and launched into a stream of Japanese, gesturing with her ladle toward the left, then waving her hand past a tall pole with paper lanterns, then pointing toward a booth shaped like a little train station, then holding up two fingers.

"I didn't catch any of that," Caius said. "Did you?"

"One word. Maybe two." Claire wrote down what she remembered in her notebook. "She said something like eki, and mae, and I think two of something. Eki means station. I'm almost sure."

They walked toward the lantern pole, and Claire kept testing her idea against what she saw. In her Japanese class at school, Ms. Joseph had taught them words for buildings, corners and station exits, and Claire had once complained that the textbook never gave her street names to memorize. Now, watching the soup woman point at the train-station booth and not at any sign at all, she began to wonder whether that missing vocabulary was not a gap in the book but a clue. Maybe streets simply did not work the way she assumed here. In class they had learned that only a few cities, like Kyoto, used street names in addresses, and everyone else navigated by landmarks and stations instead. That would explain the pointing, the two fingers, the word mae, which she was now fairly certain meant "in front of."

At the little station booth, Claire stopped a man carrying a folding table. She asked, slowly, whether the demonstration was in front of the station, on the second floor. He beamed and answered with one word, "Hai," and a thumbs up.

Stairs. Second floor. Claire led them up, and they found the room just as the calligraphy master swept ink across a sheet of paper wide as a table. The character he painted was wave, and Angelique whispered that it looked like a tsunami curling before it crashed. Claire sat down in the back row, her notebook open on her knee.

"Next festival," Caius whispered, "you're asking for the bathroom."

"Give me a week," Claire said, and started copying the character for wave.

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: French possessive words agree with the thing owned, not the owner, so "sa mère" can mean either "his mother" or "her mother."
story:
The French booth at the cultural festival smelled like butter and burnt sugar, and Olivier had been standing behind its counter for an hour with his cue cards. His class had promised Mr. Rodríguez they would run a "meet my family" station where visitors tried describing their families in full sentences, and Olivier was the one stuck talking first.

"Mon chien s'appelle Biscuit," he offered to a woman with a toddler on her hip. "Ma soeur s'appelle Camille." He was feeling decent about it until Musa slid up beside him with a grin and a paper cup of lemonade.

"Okay, test me," Musa said. "I've been studying all week. Sa mère s'appelle Madame Diallo."

"Wait, whose mother?" Olivier asked.

Musa blinked. "My mother. Obviously."

"No, I mean I can't tell. You said sa mère, and I don't know if that's your mother or somebody else's mother." Olivier looked down at his cue cards, then back up. The woman with the toddler had leaned in too, waiting.

"That's the weird part," Musa said. "Sa mère can mean his mother or her mother. Same words."

Olivier frowned. That seemed like a broken system. He tried it out on the woman. "Sa mère aime le chocolat," he said slowly, pointing at Musa. She pointed at Musa too, then shrugged, so Olivier understood her guess. But when Brynley wandered over from the face-painting booth and said the exact same sentence, pointing at no one, the woman pointed at Brynley instead.

"So the sa part follows the mother, not the person talking," Olivier said, mostly to himself. He grabbed a napkin and wrote: sa mère = his mother OR her mother. "The only way to know is to ask. Est-ce que c'est ta mère?" He aimed the question at Brynley.

"C'est ma soeur, actually," Brynley said, laughing. "But close enough."

By the afternoon the three of them had a system. When a visitor said a sentence with a possessive, Olivier would ask a follow-up question before translating, and the visitors started catching on faster. Two kids who came back for seconds of the sugar crêpes collaborated on a poster that read WHOSE? ASK! and taped it to the booth's front panel.

An older man stopped by near closing time and said he'd started a small bakery years ago, une petite boulangerie, and that his sa fille was taking it over. Olivier asked whose daughter, in French, and the man laughed and clarified, and Brynley joked that a mystery bakery run by an unknown daughter would probably go toxic from unsold bread anyway.

Mr. Rodríguez swung by at five o'clock with the leftover crêpe batter. "How did it go?"

Olivier held up the napkin, WHOSE? ASK! written under it in wobbly marker. "We figured out the system," he said. "Sa mère," he told Mr. Rodríguez, "can mean his mother or her mother."

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: In the United States, a large CDC survey found the median age of a girl's first period is about 12 years old, with a wide normal range around it.
story:
Sarah stood in aisle three of Hartley's Pharmacy, holding a small purple box and doing math in her head. Twelve. That was the number she kept landing on, because at Jadon's house last week his older sister Lena had said something Sarah couldn't stop thinking about. Lena and her cousin were comparing notes, laughing over chips, and Lena had said, "The median is around twelve, you know. Half of girls get it before that, half after, and the normal range is really wide." Her cousin had nodded and said her own first period had come at ten, while Lena had waited until she was almost fourteen, and both were normal, which had made both of them shrug like it was nothing.

Sarah's mom had sent her here for cough drops and batteries, and she'd wandered past the shelf of pads and tampons on her way to the register. She was twelve and a half, and so far nothing had happened to her, while her friend Edward's older sister had apparently needed supplies urgently at a school trip last spring. Sarah had been quietly worried that she was late, broken, or somehow behind schedule in a race she never signed up for. But Lena's numbers had given her an idea, and ideas were like currency to Sarah; she traded them with Edward and Jadon at lunch, and the good ones were worth a lot.

So she had a test. If the median was about twelve with a wide range, then asking a few trusted grown-up women when theirs started should produce very different answers, not matching ones. If they all matched, her worry was right and she was weird. If they scattered, Lena's numbers held up and Sarah was just somewhere inside a very wide normal range.

She paid for the cough drops first, then got brave. Mr. Fernando, the pharmacist who sometimes judged the school science fair, was restocking behind the counter. He was about the least scary adult she knew. "Mr. Fernando, weird question for a survey," she said. "Could you ask your wife and maybe your sister when they got their first periods? For science?" He blinked twice, then laughed so hard he emitted a snort that rattled the vitamin display. "For science, I can do that," he said. "Text me tomorrow."

The next afternoon her phone buzzed with three ages: thirteen, eleven, and almost fifteen. Scattered everywhere, exactly like the wide range Lena had described. Sarah grinned and carried the results to lunch like a trophy. Edward, who wanted to be a data scientist at some prestigious university someday, helped her chart the ages on a napkin, plus Lena and her cousin's numbers. Jadon added tick marks with his mechanical pencil and said, "It looks like a sprinkle, not a line." "Exactly," Sarah said. "Nobody's on the same schedule, and the middle is just the middle, not the deadline."

She kept the napkin folded in her backpack for a week, taking it out when the worry crept back. On Saturday she marched into aisle three again, put the purple box in the cart next to the batteries, and rolled toward checkout with her chin up. The cashier raised an eyebrow at the cough drops, the batteries, and the box, and Sarah said, "Being prepared. It's a whole science."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Most pencil cores are graphite powder mixed with clay, and adding more clay makes a harder pencil that leaves lighter marks.
story:
Harrison sat at his grandpa's kitchen table with a sketch of a lighthouse he wanted to finish before supper. He had two pencils, both yellow, both the same length, both sharpened to a fine point. One laid down dark, smudgy lines. The other barely marked the paper at all, and it was driving him crazy.

"What's wrong with this thing?" he muttered, pressing harder until the tip nearly snapped.

His friend Tori, who had come along for the afternoon, leaned over from the other side of the table, where she was glueing shells onto a picture frame. "Let me see." She drew a loop on the corner of his page with the faint pencil, then a loop with the dark one. The difference was obvious. "Same brand, even. Weird."

Harrison's first instinct was to throw the light pencil in the junk drawer, but then he turned both pencils over in his hand and looked at the tiny letters stamped near the end. One said 2B. The other said 4H. He squinted at them. "These don't match. That has to mean something."

He flipped through his grandpa's old desk dictionary, then a battered, durable art handbook with a cracked spine that had been sitting on the shelf since forever. There it was, in a paragraph about drawing supplies. He read it twice. "Tori. Listen to this. Most pencil cores are graphite powder mixed with clay, and adding more clay makes a harder pencil that leaves lighter marks."

"So the faint one isn't broken," Tori said slowly. "It's just harder. More clay in it."

Harrison nodded, but he wanted proof, not just a claim in an old book. So he tested it. He found a third pencil in the desk drawer, marked HB, and drew three lines side by side: one with the 2B, one with the HB, one with the 4H. The dark line was darkest, the HB landed exactly in between, and the hard pencil's line was faintest of all. It lined up perfectly with what the book said. His guess and the book had happened to coincide, which felt better than luck.

"It's backwards from what you'd think," Tori said. "Harder should mean darker, like harder pressing."

"That's what I thought too. But it's the opposite."

He looked at his lighthouse sketch with new eyes. The dark pencil was smearing grey dust everywhere, especially where he had tried to draw thin clouds. He took the hard pencil and lightly traced the clouds again, then the white stripes on the lighthouse tower. The faint, crisp lines made the clouds look soft and the paint look clean, better than anything he had drawn before.

That evening he showed the finished sketch to his grandpa, who held it up to the window light. "The clouds," his grandpa said. "How'd you get them so airy?"

Harrison grinned and tapped the side of his nose. "Trade secret. It's all in the clay."

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Apps must ask permission to use a phone's camera, microphone or contacts, and you can take that permission away later in the phone's settings.
story:
Paisley held her first phone in both hands, the way you hold a bird that might fly off. The family group chat was already blinking: Mom had texted "Welcome to the chat, Paisley!" with six party hats. Her thumb hovered over the keyboard. She typed, deleted, and retyped the message three times before sending "Thanks, Mom," which felt so flat compared to all those hats.

She had been a candidate for a phone since spring, and she knew exactly why she'd lost the first vote. Flashback: April, the kitchen table, her father sliding his own phone across the wood toward her. "Look at this bill," he'd said, and she had downloaded a game that quietly charged money for extra gems. The gems had been shiny and green on the screen. The bill had been thirty-one dollars, which was not shiny at all. Her father hadn't yelled. He'd just said, "Next year, maybe," and the maybe had sat in the kitchen like a smell.

Now it was next year, and she had her own phone, and she was not going to ruin it. She opened the app store and found a free flashlight app, because her room had one flickering bulb and she was tired of bumping her shin on the desk. But before it would install, a box popped up asking to use her contacts. A flashlight. Wanting her contacts. She stared at the words until her eyes watered. Why would a light need to know her aunt's phone number? She pressed Deny, half expecting the app to slam shut. It installed anyway, and the flashlight worked perfectly, a bright white circle in the dark of her cupped hands.

She texted Rosaly: "Why would a flashlight app ask for my contacts??" Rosaly replied with a shrug emoji, which helped nobody. So Paisley went digging in settings, the way she'd once dug through the garage for her missing cleat, and found a page listing every permission the phone had ever given out. Apps must ask permission to use the camera, the microphone, or the contacts, and there they all were, little switches she could flip. An app she'd tried yesterday, a voice memo thing, had the microphone switched on. She flicked it off. The switch went grey with a tiny click she felt more than heard.

At school the next morning she showed the settings page to Nigel, who leaned so close his breath fogged the screen. "Wait, you can take it back?" he said. "After you already said yes?" Paisley nodded. Mr. Singh, walking past their bench on yard duty, glanced at the screen. "Good page to know," was all he said, and kept walking.

Nigel scrolled through his own phone and groaned. A photo app had his microphone, his contacts, and his camera, all switched on like a corridor of lights nobody had turned off. "This is like acid or something," he muttered. "It's corrosive, that's the word. It just quietly eats stuff." Paisley thought about April, the green gems, the thirty-one dollars, and how quiet all of it had been until the bill came. She couldn't decide yet whether she was a careful person or just a person who'd been burned once.

"So did you text your mom back properly?" Nigel asked, still flipping switches. "Six party hats deserve more than two words."

Paisley took her phone, opened the chat, and typed: "Dear Mom, thank you for the phone. It is bright enough to blind a raccoon. Love, Paisley." She read it once, decided it counted as a paraphrase of her real feelings, and hit send.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: In 'The Wealth of Nations', published in 1776, Adam Smith pointed out that nothing is more useful than water, yet it will buy scarcely anything, while a diamond can buy a great deal.
story:
Owen had been saving since March, and by October the jar held exactly sixty-two dollars, which was supposed to be enough for a ticket to see Silverline until the price jumped to eighty-five overnight. He stood in the line outside the arena with Malorie, who had grabbed her ticket the day sales opened and kept glancing at his face like she was watching for bad news.

"Every show on the tour sold out," she said. "My mom says that's why the price went up. Too many people, not enough seats." The line inched forward under a sky that radiated cold silver light, and a scalper walked past murmuring "hundred twenty, hundred twenty," which made Owen's stomach drop. He counted heads. The line curved around the block twice, and a security guard announced that only forty tickets remained for tonight's window.

Yacine, two spots ahead, spun around when he heard them talking. "It's like this book Mr. Sow has," Yacine said. "The Wealth of Nations, from 1776, by Adam Smith. He wrote that nothing is more useful than water, yet water will buy scarcely anything, while a diamond can buy a great deal." Malorie frowned. "Water keeps you alive and a diamond just sits there. That's backwards." "That's what Smith said, though. Word for word."

Owen turned it over while the line shuffled ahead. He watched a vendor's cart at the corner, where bottled water was stacked in rows and sold for a dollar, because the cooler was full and nobody was fighting over it. Meanwhile the scalper's tickets climbed from a hundred twenty to a hundred forty as the guard's count of remaining seats dropped toward twenty. Same sidewalk, two different things, and the price followed the crowd, not the usefulness. He tested his idea out loud. "If the cooler had only three bottles left and a hundred thirsty people, water would cost more than a ticket." Malorie said, "You'd pay it, too, if you'd been standing out here since six."

When the window opened, the last forty tickets went in eleven minutes, and Owen was nine people too far back. The guard waved him off with a shake of his head, and the scalper raised his sign again: one hundred fifty. Owen looked at his sixty-two dollars, then at the water cart, where the vendor was now selling bottles three for a dollar because almost everyone had already gone inside and nobody wanted them.

"Hey," Owen said to the vendor. "If I help you fold up the empties and haul the cart to your truck, can I have one of those bottles?" The man laughed and agreed, and Owen worked fast, stacking crates while the crowd inside roared at the opening song.
