He carried his free bottle back to where Malorie waited by the doors, holding it up like a trophy. "One dollar off, three for a dollar, or free with labor," he said. "Turns out that's the whole ticket market too." Malorie hugged the bottle against her jacket and pulled him toward the side door, where the sound leaked out warm and enormous. "You can hear the encore from right here," she said. "Come on, they're starting."

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: When a dialogue tag follows a spoken sentence, the sentence ends with a comma inside the quotation marks instead of a period, as in "I'm ready," she said.
story:
Arthur sat at the corner table of the public library with his notebook open to page three of a story about two kids who find a buried box in a creek bed. Every line where someone spoke looked wrong to him, and he could not say why. He had written: "I'm going to dig it up." said Marco. The period sat there before the tag like a pebble in his shoe.

Hayden slid into the chair across from him and read the page upside down. "Mr. Whitaker circled every single one of these in my draft," Hayden said, pulling out his own paper, which was marked in red. Arthur leaned over. The circles all sat around periods that came before "said Marco" or "she said." On one line, though, there was no circle, and Arthur noticed that line ended with a comma instead.

"That one's different," Arthur said, tapping it. "Look. She said, 'I'm ready,' and then the tag, and there's a comma inside the quotes." He tested the idea on his own draft, reading each line aloud. When a tag like "said Marco" came after the spoken words, he changed the period to a comma and tucked it inside the quotation marks. When the quote stood alone, the period stayed. He marked eleven changes in pencil.

Mr. Whitaker came by with a stack of poetry books for the writing club that met at the next table. He dropped one in front of Omer. "Find a luminous stanza for the display board," he said. "Something that lights up the page." Omer flipped through and read quietly, hunting for four or five lines that shone.

Arthur still had one problem left. His story had no climax. The kids dug up the box, opened it, and found old letters, and then it just stopped. He read the pages again and crossed out the last two paragraphs. Instead, he wrote a new ending where the box had to be opened before the creek water rose, and Marco dropped the key through a grate at the worst possible moment. He read it to Hayden.

"That part where he drops the key," Hayden said, "I actually held my breath." Arthur drew a box around that paragraph and labeled it climax, then copied the whole thing onto clean paper, commas tucked inside every quotation mark, and carried it to the front desk to ask the librarian about the contest for young writers. She pointed at the bin marked "Short Stories, Ages 11 to 13." Arthur dropped his pages in.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: In the Dutch Republic, prices for rare tulip bulbs soared in the winter of 1636 to 1637 and then collapsed in February 1637, when buyers stopped showing up.
story:
Ellie raced down Mr. Murphy's driveway so fast she nearly skidded into a box of old board games. The garage sale had opened at eight, and she had been awake since six, because the whole school had been talking about one thing all week: Glacier Dragons cards. The shiny ones were nearly impossible to find, and yesterday Braelyn had traded three regular cards just for one corner of a torn one. If Mr. Murphy had any in this garage, Ellie intended to be first.

She dug through a shoebox of cards, and there it was: a Glacier Dragon, silver-edged, sitting in a plastic sleeve. Her heart hammered. "How much for this one?" she asked.

Mr. Murphy squinted at it. "That one's special, I hear. Ten dollars."

Ten dollars! The regular cards were a quarter each, stacked in bundles by the door. "Why is this one so much more?" she asked, mostly to stall while she counted her money. She had nine dollars and a bus token.

"Because everybody wants it and there's hardly any of them," Mr. Murphy said. "Same thing happened with tulips once. In the Dutch Republic, prices for rare tulip bulbs soared in the winter of 1636 to 1637, and then they collapsed in February 1637, when buyers stopped showing up." He tapped the card. "My grandfather told me that story, and I never forgot it."

Ellie handed over nine dollars, and Mr. Murphy let her have it, saying getting here first at eight in the morning ought to count for something. She felt like she'd won a lottery. On the driveway, Alfred appeared, breathless, waving a five-dollar bill. "Is that a Glacier Dragon? I'll give you my lunch money for it! Braelyn will trade you her whole binder!"

Ellie's mind spun. Lots of buyers, hardly any cards, prices shooting up. She devised a plan on the spot: she would take Braelyn's binder trade this afternoon, then sell the extra shiny cards at Saturday's swap meet while everyone still wanted them. Timing felt crucial. If she waited too long, people might stop showing up, the way they had with the tulips, and the whole thing would fall apart.

But she never got the chance. Monday morning, Alfred shrugged past her in the hallway and said, "Nobody's trading Glacier Dragons anymore. There's this new space game now." By the flagpole, Braelyn was already swapping her entire binder to a sixth grader for a handful of rocket cards.

Ellie stood there, the silver dragon still in her backpack. Then she turned around, marched back to Mr. Murphy's house, and knocked on the garage door. "Do you have any cards with planets on them?" she asked. "I have nine dollars, and I'd like first pick."

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: Section 1 of the Canadian Charter says its rights are subject to reasonable limits that can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society.
story:
Rebecca pressed her nose to the glass door of the courthouse and watched people hurry up the wide steps with their coats flapping. Her class was there for the poster contest about the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, and the winner would read their explanation out loud in Courtroom Four. Rebecca wanted that spot. She had picked section 2, freedom of expression, and she had drawn a giant open mouth with words pouring out of it like a river.

On the steps, Salome was arguing with Sahil, who was waving his own poster. "Freedom of expression means anyone can say anything," Sahil said. "Anything at all. That's the whole point."

Salome dug through her backpack and pulled out a curled copy of the Charter. "Read the top part out loud," she said, "before your list of rights even starts."

Sahil squinted at the small print. "Section 1 of the Canadian Charter says its rights are subject to reasonable limits that can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society." He frowned. "That's a mouthful."

Rebecca felt something click, like a puzzle piece turning over. So the rights weren't a door swinging wild on its hinges. They were a door with a frame around them. She wondered: limits? Who decided what counted as reasonable? She couldn't see the rule working the way you could see a scoreboard, but maybe you could test it, the way you test whether a floor is frozen by pressing one boot down first.

Inside, Mr. Chea, whose classroom was next door to theirs and who had come to supervise the trip, gathered everyone near the tall wooden doors of Courtroom Four. "Two minutes to fix your posters," he said. Rebecca crouched in the corner with her river of words and thought hard. She borrowed a pencil from Salome and drew a thin fence right along the riverbank. The words still poured, but now they stayed inside something.

When her name was called, she stood at the front of the courtroom, where a judge usually sat, and held up the poster. "Freedom of expression means I can say what I think," she said. "But section 1 of the Charter says the rights are subject to reasonable limits that can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society. So my river of words has a riverbank. The words are still free to flow, but they can't flood somebody else."

A woman in the second row, who had been fixing her scarf, leaned toward her friend and whispered, "That kid just explained it better than the news does."

Sahil raised his hand even though there was no teacher asking. "So I couldn't say anything at all? Not even a joke?"

"A joke, sure," Rebecca said. "Not a flood."

Mr. Chea read the winner's name into the microphone, and it was hers. Walking out past the security guard, poster tube under her arm, she caught up with Salome at the big glass doors.

"Can a rule you can't see still be a real rule?" she asked.

Salome shrugged. "You drew it a fence. Now I can see it."

Rebecca laughed and tapped the tube. "Riverbanks, fences, whatever works."

activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
knowledge_domain: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
fact: Mise en place is a French cooking term meaning 'putting in place': preparing and measuring every ingredient before you start cooking.
story:
Max stood in the kitchen on Saturday morning with three recipes spread across the counter and a plan that felt enormous: rice, curry, and flatbread, all hot and ready at the exact same moment. His mom had agreed to judge the results at one o'clock, and Sammy and Shae were coming over to eat. He wanted this meal to be coherent, everything landing on the table together like a real dinner, not a staggered mess of one dish steaming while another sat cold.

He started the onions first because the curry was the longest job. They sizzled in the pan, turning golden, and that was exactly when he realized he had no idea where the cumin was. He dug through the spice cupboard while the onions spat and darkened behind him. By the time he found the jar, the onions had turned black at the edges and the kitchen smelled bitter. He scraped them into the compost and stood there staring at the empty pan.

"Why did that happen?" he asked the air. It wasn't that he couldn't cook. It was that he kept stopping to hunt for things. He texted Shae, whose family cooked every night, and she answered fast: "Mise en place. It's a French cooking term meaning 'putting in place.' You prep and measure every ingredient before you start." Max read it twice. He grabbed a marker and wrote a big amendment across his handwritten schedule at the top: PREP EVERYTHING FIRST.

So he did. He measured the rice into a bowl, chopped every onion, measured out the turmeric, cumin, and salt into tiny dishes, mixed the flour and water for the flatbread, and lined everything up along the counter like a parade. Then he sat with his timer and worked the timing backward, which felt like solving a puzzle he couldn't see the answer to until he tested it. The curry needed forty minutes, the rice twenty-five, the flatbread only ten including resting the dough. So the rice would go in when the curry had fifteen minutes left, and the dough would hit the pan last, while everything else bubbled and steamed.

When Sammy arrived early, Max was already sliding the first flatbread onto the hot pan. "You look like a TV chef," Sammy said, watching the little bowls of spices all measured and waiting. Max flipped the flatbread, watched it puff, and moved it to a warm plate without hunting for a single thing.

The timer beeped and Max lifted lids all at once. Fluffy rice, thick curry, golden bread, all steaming together. His mom took one bite, then another, then nodded slowly and reached for the flatbread. "Okay, chef," she said. "When's dinner tomorrow?"

activity: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
knowledge_domain: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
fact: In Shakespeare's English, he or she verbs often end in -eth or -th, so doth means does and hath means has.
story:
The clock above the whiteboard gave Ava's group exactly eleven minutes, and Ms. Wright had already circled their desk twice like a shark wearing sensible shoes. Their task sat on the handout: take the scene from Romeo and Juliet and rewrite every speech in modern English, then perform it in front of the class. Delaney had turned "Wherefore art thou Romeo" into "Why are you Romeo" without trouble. Maximiliano had managed "do not swear by the moon" easily enough. But now they were stuck, because the next line read "She hath not seen the change of fourteen years," and nobody knew what to do with that word.

"Hath," Maximiliano said, poking it with his pencil as if it might bite. "That's not even a word. That's a typo with confidence."

"It's a word," Delaney said, "it's just an old word. The question is which old word." She looked at Ava, who was supposed to be the group's ideas person since the incident with the volcano poster, when Ava had single-handedly saved their science grade. Ava stared at the line. Hath. She scanned up the page and found "doth" in an earlier speech, then "thou dost," and then, further down, "she doth teach the torches to burn bright." She noticed something: every time the character was he or she, the verb grew that little th on the end. Thou got st. You got nothing. It was a pattern, and patterns, unlike humidity, could be trusted.

"I think it's a grammar thing," Ava said, tapping the page. "He or she verbs end in eth or th. So doth means does." She pointed at the line. "And hath means has. So it's just, she has not seen the change of fourteen years. She's not fourteen yet."

Delaney gasped like Ava had revealed a family secret. "That's it! That's so boring and normal!" Maximiliano wrote "she is not even fourteen" on the paraphrase sheet with a flourish, then leaned his chair back so far that Ava had to grab his sleeve to keep him from tipping over, which would have eroded what little dignity their group had left, since they were already endangered by the two minutes remaining.

"One minute!" Ms. Wright called, and the smell of old paperback pages mixed with the sharp marker scent of the whiteboard as they ran through their lines once, fast, Ava whisper-correcting "hath means has" every time Maximiliano hesitated. When Ms. Wright pointed at them, they stood up in front of the class in their too-warm corner of the classroom by the radiator, and Maximiliano delivered "She is not even fourteen years old, folks" with the gravity of a man announcing his residence had burned down, and someone in the second row actually laughed, which counted as a victory.

After class, Delaney caught Ava at the door. "So tomorrow, when we get the sonnet, you're doing all the weird words."

"Deal," Ava said, "but if there's another volcano, you're carrying the baking soda."

activity: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
knowledge_domain: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
fact: The Grand Canyon is 277 miles (446 kilometers) long and over a mile deep at its deepest point.
story:
The planetarium projector emitted a slow river of stars across the dome, and Anna slid down in her seat, trying to make her nervousness settle with the dark. In two days she had to give a science talk on how a river carves a canyon over millions of years, and she still could not picture it. Water seemed too soft to cut anything.

"Sit up," whispered Ariel beside her. "Mr. Kang is going to call on people."

He did not call on her, but he did something worse. He walked the aisles while the dome showed the surface of Mars, so desolate that not even a blade of grass broke the red plain, and said that anyone who wanted bonus points could stand after the show and explain a landform of their choice. Anna's hand went up before she had decided anything.

After the lights came back on, she stood in front of the class with her knees shaking and began with the Colorado River. She said that the river carries sand and pebbles, and that the grinding of that sediment against rock wears the channel down, bit by bit, while the water also carries the loose material away and drops it downstream. She had the concept right, she was almost sure, but a hand shot up near the back. Nikki.

"How deep even is a real canyon?" Nikki asked. "Like, deeper than a swimming pool?"

Anna opened her mouth and nothing came out. Then she remembered the number she had read three times on the bus that morning, because she hadn't believed it the first two times. "The Grand Canyon is 277 miles long," she said, "and over a mile deep at its deepest point. That's 446 kilometers." She held her hands a mile apart, which looked ridiculous, and some kids laughed, so she pointed at the floor. "Imagine our school at the bottom, and the mile of rock that used to be above it, all carried off grain by grain."

"Grain by grain for how long?" Nikki asked.

"Millions of years," Anna said. "That's the whole point. A river is slow, but it never stops."

Mr. Kang nodded once, the small nod he saved for answers he liked, and told her well done. Walking out under the afternoon sun, Ariel bumped her shoulder. "You turned red up there."

Anna grinned. "Only for the first mile."

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Japan, slurping noodles such as ramen and soba is considered acceptable at the table rather than rude.
story:
Nicolas stood on Ayat's porch holding a box of oranges his dad had bought on his commute home, and he could not remember whether he was supposed to knock or ring or just walk in. His rain jacket had turned out to be porous in the storm, so his sleeves were damp and the cardboard was going soft, which made the whole thing worse. Ayat opened the door before he could decide, and the first thing she said was "Shoes off, that's the rule here." Nicolas looked down at the row of slippers by the door, then at his wet socks, and laughed. "Good thing I wore clean ones," he said, stepping out of his sneakers.

The kitchen smelled like broth and ginger. Ayat's mother was lifting a huge pot of ramen to the table, and her father was telling Nicolas's dad, who had come up behind him, that the family used to run a small noodle shop before the highway moved and took away half their revenue. "Everyone commuted right past us for years," he said, shaking his head. "Now we just cook for friends." He handed Nicolas a deep bowl with chopsticks on the side, and Nicolas noticed something strange right away.

Everyone slurped. Ayat slurped. Her mother slurped, quite loudly, while reading the label on a jar of chili oil. Her father slurped so hard the noodles vanished in one long pull. Nicolas froze with his chopsticks halfway to his mouth. At home he had been told, more than once, that slurping was rude, and he did not want to be rude here either. But he noticed something else too: the more the family slurped, the faster the noodles disappeared, and the noodles were steaming hot. The quiet way he was eating meant each mouthful sat and cooled before he dared swallow it.

He decided to test his idea. He took one strand, breathed in, and slurped. The noodle zipped up cool and perfect, and his mouth filled with broth. Ayat grinned at him across the table. "Better, right?" she said. "Slurping's fine with noodles. It's just how it's done." Nicolas slurped again, louder this time, and Ayat's father raised his glass of tea like he was giving a toast.

When the bowls were empty, Ayat's mother pressed the last orange from the box into Nicolas's hands for the walk home. At the door, Ayat helped him work his damp sneakers back onto the right feet. "Next time bring your brother," she called from the porch as he stepped out into the drizzle, and Nicolas waved the orange at her.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Most travelers find jet lag harder to adjust to after flying east than after flying west.
story:
Gabriella had felt fine the day they flew to the beach, and that was the part that confused her. The flight west had taken half a day, and still she had slept like a normal person that first night, and by morning she was digging in the sand before her dad had even found the sunscreen. Now, three days after flying home east, she was still waking at four in the morning and dragging through every afternoon, and on Monday she had to give her science fair talk at 8:15 sharp. Monday was two days away.

She called Martha from the kitchen, phone wedged between ear and shoulder while she assembled a sandwich that was at least nutritious, turkey and tomatoes and whole grain bread. "I don't get it," she said. "Same plane, same length of flight, one direction I'm fine and the other I'm a zombie."

"It's jet lag," Martha said. "My cousin gets it every time they fly to Europe."

"That's the thing," Gabriella said. "I had jet lag going out too, maybe, but it barely bothered me. Coming home it's like being sick." She looked at her notebook, where she had written two columns: OUT, WEST, FINE. HOME, EAST, MISERABLE. If it were just the flying, both trips should feel the same. Something about the direction itself seemed to matter. She had a candidate theory, scrawled at the bottom of the page: east is worse.

She needed evidence, so she tried an experiment on herself. The problem, she reasoned, was that her body still thought it was three hours earlier than the clock claimed, so bedtime felt impossible at nine. On Friday night she skipped screens, closed her curtains, and lay in the dark anyway, even though she wasn't sleepy. It was awful for about an hour. Then she slept until almost seven, the latest she'd managed since landing.

Saturday she called Martha again, then Jameson, who had a suggestion. "Ask Mr. Whitaker," he said. "He flew to Japan once, remember, for that chess thing." Mr. Whitaker lived two houses down, and when she caught him watering his roses he laughed at her question. "Going over, east, I was a wreck for days," he said. "Coming home, west, I was myself by the second morning. Almost unfair, isn't it." He was still talking about his tournament when she left, but she had what she came for. Her two columns matched his story exactly. Flying east was harder to recover from than flying west, and apparently most travelers found the same, which made her feel less like a broken machine and more like a person with a bad travel direction.

Sunday night she went to bed at eight-thirty, early but not crazy. Monday morning her eyes opened at six-fifteen, one click before the alarm, and she lay still for a moment listening to it. She ate her toast standing up, tucked her note cards into her backpack, and ran the talk in her head one last time on the walk to school. "Good morning," she began, out loud, alone on the sidewalk. "My project is about sleep, travel, and a pattern I tested on myself."

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: A pet microchip is about the size of a grain of rice and holds an ID number that a scanner reads to find the owner's contact details.
story:
Luke carried the cardboard carrier out of the shelter with both hands, feeling the small weight shift inside it every few steps. His new rabbit, whom he had already named Clover, nosed at the air holes in the corner. The shelter worker had put a folder of care papers in his backpack, and Luke had read the feeding page twice on the bus so he would not forget anything by the time he got home.

He cut through Hollow Creek Park because the path ran parallel to the fence along the creek, and Clover seemed calmer when the carrier swayed gently instead of jostling on the sidewalk. Near the fountain he ran into Kaila, who crouched down to peek through the air holes. "A rabbit," she said. "Nice. I confess I thought your first pet would be something loud, like a parrot."

Before Luke could answer, a small brown terrier trotted out from under a bench, muddy and shivering, with no collar at all. It circled them once and then sat at Kaila's feet as if it had been waiting there all afternoon. "It's lost," Kaila said. "Somebody has to be looking for it." Luke looked around the park, at the empty benches and the far-off swing set, and thought about how the dog could not tell them anything. No tag meant no name, no address, nothing.

Then he remembered a poster by the shelter door. "Dogs get microchips," he said slowly, working it out as he spoke. "My cousin's dog had one. It's about the size of a grain of rice, and it holds an ID number that a scanner reads to find the owner's contact details." Kaila stood up. "Mr. Esposito," she said. "He volunteers at the shelter on weekends, and he walks in this park every day at four." It was ten past four.

They found Mr. Esposito by the duck pond, and he had a scanner with him, a small box like a remote control. He waved it over the terrier's shoulders, and a number appeared on the little screen. "There we go," he said, and tapped the number into his phone. While they waited, Luke set the carrier down on the grass and let Clover sniff a dandelion leaf through the holes, declaring a brief truce between his worry for the terrier and his excitement about his own new pet.

A woman came running across the soccer field before the dandelion leaf was finished, calling a name that made the terrier's ears shoot up. The dog sprang into her arms, tail whirling, and she thanked them three times and shook everyone's hand, even Luke's, who was still holding the carrier. "You did exactly the right thing," Mr. Esposito told him, pocketing the scanner. Luke picked up the carrier and walked home along the creek, and through the air holes he could hear Clover crunching the last of the leaf.

activity: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark
knowledge_domain: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark
fact: Glazing means brushing a thin transparent wash over a layer that is completely dry, so the colours mix optically instead of blending together on the paper.
story:
Asher wanted his portrait of the school librarian to look real, the way the ones in the museum catalogue did, with cheeks that had shadow and warmth instead of one flat colour. Ms. Hoffmann had written one word on the board at the start of art club: glazing. She refused to say more. "You'll figure it out," she said, and went to help Brynley unstick a jammed paint tube.

He had painted a pale wash of peach over the whole face and let it dry while he sketched the eyes. Then he mixed a thin rosy wash for the shadow under the cheekbone. Annika leaned over from the next table. "Are you sure it's dry?" she asked.

Asher touched the corner of the paper with his fingertip. It felt dry at the edge, cool and smooth, and he decided the middle must be dry too. He brushed the rose wash across the cheek. The moment the brush touched, the peach underneath bloomed up into it, swirling like ink dropped in water, and the cheek turned a muddy brown-grey blob. His abrupt stroke had dragged the damp layer into the new one, and now nothing was where he had put it.

Annika winced. "That happened to my apple on Tuesday. I painted the highlight over red that was still wet underneath and it all ran together."

"So the surface can feel dry but be wet below," Asher said slowly. He looked at the ruined cheek, then at Ms. Hoffmann's word on the board. He tried the idea out loud. "Glazing. Maybe glazing means brushing a thin transparent wash over a layer that's completely dry, so the colours mix in your eye instead of on the paper." Annika tilted her head, and Brynley abandoned her paint tube to listen.

"Mix in your eye," Brynley repeated. "Like the purple you get when you hold blue film over red film?"

Asher nodded. His impatience had been the real adversary, not the paint. He fetched a hair dryer from the supply shelf and, since Brynley's portrait needed the same treatment, they collaborated, aiming the warm air at each other's papers in turns while the clock ticked toward the end of club. When his page finally felt dry all the way through, dry as toast, he loaded the thinnest possible wash of rose.

The brush glided over the cheek without a single bloom. Underneath, the peach showed through the transparent rose, and where the two overlapped the shadow looked warm and alive. Annika leaned in close to his paper and said, "It's like the colours are stacked instead of stirred."

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: In a 1950 study of a student housing complex at MIT, Leon Festinger and colleagues found residents most often became friends with the people who lived closest to them.
story:
The new house smelled like paint and cardboard, and Owen stood alone in the middle of his empty bedroom, holding the last box from the truck. In it he found his dad's old college books, which must have gotten mixed in with his stuff. One was thick and boring looking until a folded page fell out. On it, a paragraph was underlined in pencil. It said that in 1950, Leon Festinger and his colleagues studied a student housing complex at MIT, and found that the residents most often became friends with the people who lived closest to them. Owen read it twice. His dad had drawn a little arrow in the margin beside it, pointing at the word "closest."

Owen carried the book downstairs, where his mom was taping box flaps in the kitchen. "Did you underline this?" he asked. She squinted at the page and laughed. "That's from my first year at college. I marked it because I'd made friends with the girl across the hall and nobody else." She went back to her tape. Owen stood there thinking. His two best friends back home, Mckinley and Joy, had lived one street over and two streets over. He had never noticed that before. The concept seemed almost too simple, but the book said a whole complex full of MIT students had proved it.

So he tested it. He went out the front door and looked at the house directly next door, the one with the moving van still parked outside it too. Whoever lived there was also brand new, which felt like cheating on the experiment somehow, but closest was closest. He knocked, his heart doing something acute and jumpy in his chest. A boy about his age opened the door, still holding a rolled-up poster of a soccer player. "You live next door?" the boy said. "I'm Sanjay." Owen said his name and, feeling awkward, held up the thick book like it could portray a reason for the visit. "My dad's book says people usually become friends with whoever lives closest," he said. "So I figured I should knock on your door before anyone else's."

Sanjay considered this. "That's weird," he said. "But my mom said the same thing yesterday. She picked this house partly because the school's a two-minute walk." He looked back over his shoulder at a wall of boxes. "Want to see my room? It's the one with the best window."

They spent the afternoon unpacking Sanjay's shelf of games and arguing about which one to play first. Owen learned that Sanjay had moved three times already and had a system: he always found the nearest kid before the first week was over, because after that everyone already had plans. "Does the book say anything about a time limit?" Sanjay asked. Owen checked. It did not, which meant they would have to figure that part out themselves. That felt okay. In fact, it felt like the beginning of something. Sanjay tossed him a controller and pointed at the second spot on the couch. "That one's yours," he said. "It's the closest one."

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Setting an account to private limits who can see your posts, but anyone you have already accepted as a follower can still copy or share what they see.
story:
Benjamin had one goal on Saturday: post the photo of his catapult launching a marshmallow across the kitchen before Hank could claim the idea was his. He sat at the computer, opened the app, and hovered over the button. His account was set to private. Only followers could see his posts, and he knew every follower on his list, more or less. He clicked post and went to get a snack.

By the time he came back, a stranger had commented. The account was called marshmallow_fan_2009, and it had written, "Nice catapult. Does your mom know about the ceiling stain?" Benjamin stared at the screen. His mom definitely did not know about the ceiling stain. He checked the photo again. The stain was barely visible in the corner, behind the fridge, which meant somebody had looked closely, and somebody was not on his follower list, because the account was private, or at least it was supposed to be.

He opened his follower list and went through it like a detective, or like a kid with homework avoidance skills, which amounted to the same concentration. There was Mario, his best friend since kindergarten. There was his cousin. There was Ms. Kaur, his neighbour, who followed everyone on the street so she could see whose gardens won prizes. And there was a kid named Dylan from summer camp two years ago, whom Benjamin had accepted because it seemed rude not to. Dylan had never once commented. Suspicious.

Benjamin messaged Mario first. "Did you share my catapult post?" Mario replied with a photo of himself shrugging so hard his shoulders were in the frame. Not Mario, then. Benjamin tested his theory another way. He posted a picture of his left shoe with the caption "Top secret test post." Fourteen minutes later, marshmallow_fan_2009 commented, "Size five. Nice laces." Only followers could see it, and one of those followers had to be passing things along. He wrote to Dylan: "Hey, did you share my posts with anybody?" The typing dots appeared, disappeared, appeared again, and then Dylan's whole account vanished from his follower list, which was its own kind of confession.

Benjamin sat back. He had learned two things. First, setting an account to private limits who can see your posts, but anyone you have already accepted as a follower can still copy or share what they see. He had assumed private meant sealed, like a vault, and it turned out it was more like a club with a talkative member. Second, marshmallow_fan_2009 knew too much, and he did not intend to abandon the mystery there. He was already drafting a new post for tomorrow: a photo of a blank wall, captioned "The marshmallow was here." If the stranger commented on that, the wall, at least, could keep a secret.

From the kitchen, his mom called, "Whose marshmallow is stuck to my ceiling?"

"Controversial question," Benjamin shouted back, and closed the laptop.

activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
knowledge_domain: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
fact: When cooking several dishes for one meal, start with the one that takes longest and plan backward from the time you want to eat.
story:
Xavier spread three recipe cards on the kitchen counter like playing cards: rice, curry, flatbread. Lionel and Lauralie were arriving at seven o'clock sharp, and his mother had left for her shift with one instruction, spoken through the car window: dinner has to be on the table when you promised it. He checked the clock. Four forty-five. Plenty of time, he thought, and slid the curry pot onto the stove first because curry sounded like the main event.

By five thirty the curry was bubbling, and it needed forty more minutes. Then he read the rice card properly and felt his stomach drop. Rice, thirty-five minutes. Flatbread, twenty minutes to mix and cook, plus forty minutes for the dough to rest. He grabbed a pencil and started doing the math out loud. "If I work forward, I'll finish the curry at six ten, the rice whenever, and the bread who knows when. That's all wrong." He stared at the clock, wondering if there was a rule hiding underneath all these numbers.

Then it clicked, the way a puzzle piece clicks. "Start with the one that takes longest," he said slowly, "and plan backward from the time you want to eat." He wrote 7:00 at the top of a page and worked downward. Flatbread dough needed to rest starting at six, rice on the stove by five twenty-five, curry, already going, could sit and wait once it was done. His whole schedule rearranged itself in his head like runners moving into parallel lanes, each dish with its own track toward seven o'clock.

He mixed the flatbread dough and set it to rest, then started the rice at exactly five twenty-five. But when he glanced at the dough bowl, a cold feeling hit him. The dough had shrunk slightly, sagging in the middle. Had it failed? His reflex was to panic and throw it out, but instead he poked it with a finger. It sprang back. Whatever had happened, the dough was still alive and working. Maybe, he thought, that's exactly what resting dough is supposed to do. He decided to trust it and kept going.

At six fifty, the doorbell rang. Lauralie burst in first, nose in the air. "Something smells amazing. Is that curry?" Lionel followed, holding a bag of mango chutney like a trophy. "You actually cooked all this yourself?" "Mostly myself," Xavier admitted, and told them about his schedule, the pencil marks still visible on the page by the stove. Lauralie picked it up. "You wrote the ending first," she said. "Seven o'clock, and then everything backward from there. That's clever."

The rice was perfectly timed, the curry hot, and the flatbread came off the pan in blistered golden rounds just as the clock touched seven. Xavier set the last one on the plate and stood back. "Dinner," he announced, "is exactly on time." Lionel reached for a flatbread and grinned. "Then what are we waiting for?"

activity: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
knowledge_domain: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
fact: In meeting procedure, a quorum is the minimum number of members who must be present for the group's decisions to count.
story:
Ariana taped the agenda to the side of the slide tower at 3:45, right where everyone would see it when they climbed the playground steps. The Skate Spot Club had nine members, and today's meeting was supposed to decide how to spend the fifty dollars they'd earned washing cars. She had written three items on the agenda in her neatest print: new grip tape, a repair kit, and the ramp fund. Her mother had reminded her that morning to enforce the order of the list so nobody's topic got skipped, and Ariana intended to do exactly that.

Only Corey and Brooks had arrived by four o'clock, both of them still holding their boards. It seemed logical to start anyway, since the two of them wanted the same thing she did, the repair kit. "All in favor?" she asked, and three hands went up. She wrote the result in her notebook and was underlining it when Brooks squinted at the page.

"Hold on," he said. "Where's everyone else? Marcy texted me she'd be late because her little brother has a doctor thing about the cartilage in his knee, and the others are coming from detention."

Before Ariana could answer, three more members stomped up the wood chips, and a girl named only in Ariana's mind as the loudest one pointed at the notebook. "You voted without us? That doesn't count. You can't just decide with half the club gone."

Ariana's face went hot, but instead of arguing, she turned back a page in her notebook. At the last meeting, Mr. Campbell, the neighbor who let them use his garage for storage, had watched them argue for twenty minutes about nothing and then said, "Look up quorum, kids. It'll save you some grief." She had looked it up, and the word was sitting right there in her notes: a quorum is the minimum number of members who must be present for the group's decisions to count. She checked the club rules they'd written in September. Nine members, quorum of five.

"We didn't have a quorum," she said, crossing out the vote. "Only three of us were here. The decision doesn't count."

The loudest one, whose name was actually just what everyone called her because she was always first to speak, folded her arms anyway. "How do we know that's real and not something you made up to redo the vote?"

"Read it yourself." Ariana handed her the notebook and the rules sheet, then climbed two steps up the slide tower so the rest of them could gather below. "Next time we start with a head count. Five or more, we vote. Under five, we talk but we wait. That's fair, isn't it?"

Corey, who had been quiet the whole time, raised his hand. "Can I add something to the agenda? Marcy's brother's knee is why she's late, and the ramp fund money could go toward, like, pads and stuff for people who don't have any."

Ariana wrote it under item three, in the exact spot where it would come up after the repairs. When Marcy finally arrived, breathless with her helmet still on, five more members were counted, the quorum was met, and the vote happened again with everybody's hand in the air.

"Repair kit," Ariana announced, "and four dollars left over to start the pad fund." Corey grinned and slid down the slide, and Marcy raced him to the swings.
